args.key_findings: 1) approach_bonus dominates reward: episode_sum_mean=222.05, 99.2% signed share, 99.2% magnitude share — the policy essentially learns only from this component. 2) progress_reward (1.35, 0.6%) and landing_safety_penalty (0.26, 0.1%) are negligible, meaning the agent receives almost no gradient from distance-progress or safety violations. 3) Despite this imbalance, termination rate is high (19/20) and mean episode length is 446.4, suggesting the task is solved but reward shaping is severely miscalibrated.
args.component_anomalies: approach_bonus is a dominant outlier at 99.2% share — its coefficient (2.0) combined with multiplicative gating (prox × speed × angle) creates a reward magnitude ~164× larger than progress_reward per episode. landing_safety_penalty is near-zero (0.1% share) because its coefficients (0.03, 0.02, 0.03) are too small relative to approach_bonus. The three components operate at entirely different scales.
args.mechanism_hypothesis: The reward surface is effectively single-component: approach_bonus saturates near the target, creating a steep local gradient that overpowers the per-step progress signal. Because progress_reward contributes only 0.6% of total magnitude, the policy cannot meaningfully learn distance-minimization early in trajectories — it only learns to enter the approach_bonus activation zone, then fine-tunes locally. This explains why original_env_reward (0.058) is far below generated_reward (0.717): the shaped bonus dominates, but the bonus gradient is spatially narrow.
args.decision_implication: EDIT approach_bonus: reduce its coefficient (currently 2.0) and/or remove multiplicative gating so it no longer dwarfs progress_reward. The goal is to bring component magnitude shares into rough balance (e.g., no single component >60%) so the policy receives usable gradient from all three signals. Keep the reward structure intact — just recalibrate weights.
